header .tagline: Roughly 80 percent of the effects come from 20 percent of the causes.
header .subtitle: Vilfredo Pareto noticed in 1896 that 80% of Italy’s land was owned by 20% of its people. The pattern recurs across software, support, performance, and product strategy — most of the value comes from a small fraction of the input. Knowing which 20% is the whole game.
.law-origin .body-text: Vilfredo Pareto was an Italian economist and sociologist. In 1896 he observed that roughly 80% of Italy’s land belonged to 20% of its people; management thinker Joseph Juran later generalized the pattern as the 80/20 rule and named it for Pareto.

Pareto trained as an engineer, worked for a railway company and ran an ironworks before turning to economics at the University of Lausanne. His broader work on elite circulation influenced sociology for a century; the 80/20 shorthand came from quality-management pioneer Joseph Juran, who called it ‘the vital few and the trivial many.’
.law-content .law-desc: A small share of causes produces most of the effect. The exact ratio isn’t sacred — 70/30, 90/10 — but the imbalance is. In product, design, and engineering, finding the high-leverage minority is where the work pays for itself.

.card h3: The Hot Path Carries the Cost
AI Makes the Long Tail Cheap
.card .desc: Pareto was an Italian economist studying land ownership in 1896. He noticed about 80% of the land sat with 20% of the people — and, as the story goes, saw the same lopsided distribution in the pea pods in his garden. The pattern turned out to be everywhere, and the name stuck.

Microsoft’s Office team famously found that most users never touched most of the menus. The same shape recurs in nearly every product: a small core of features carries most of the engagement, and the rest sits unused — sometimes purposefully, often accidentally.

When everything looks important, the right move is usually to figure out which 20% of the backlog drives 80% of the outcome. MVP, roadmaps, and quarterly OKRs all rely on Pareto reasoning — picking the small set of bets that will carry most of the result.

Profile any production system and you almost always find the same shape: a small fraction of the code (or queries, or assets) is responsible for most of the time. Premature optimization is wasted everywhere else — but on the hot path, the math pays back massively.

Microsoft’s crash data and countless support queues show the same lopsidedness in crashes and tickets. A handful of bugs cause the majority of the user-visible misery; the rest are long-tail. Triage by impact, not by submission order.

Chris Anderson’s “long tail” is the warning: aggregate enough of the unused 80% and you sometimes find a market larger than the head. Amazon and Spotify both built businesses on it. Pareto tells you where to focus first, not which markets to abandon.

A naïve read of Pareto is “cut the 80% no one uses.” But unused features often serve a few critical users — accessibility, accountants, admins, oncall. Before cutting, segment by who, not just by how many. The 20% of features the bottom 5% relies on is usually load-bearing.

The principle is most useful as a habit. Before any review, ask: which 20% of users, screens, tasks, or errors carries 80% of the weight here? It rarely answers the whole question — but it almost always reorders the work in a way that pays off.

Pareto was partly a statement about cost: the 80% wasn’t worth serving because each unit was too expensive. Models flip that — translating, summarizing, supporting, or designing for one obscure case now costs nearly the same as one common case. The unused 80% gets reachable.

Models invert Pareto in a sneakier way too. They’re great at the 80% common case and worst at the 20% edge — but they sound equally confident about both. The remaining failure modes are exactly the ones that hurt: rare, plausible, and unverified.

.ai-divider h3: The Pareto Principle in the Age of AI
.ai-divider p: AI changes the math of the long tail — the 80% of edge cases that used to be too expensive to serve are now within reach.
.apply-list li: Quarterly planning starts with a backlog of ninety items and every team insists their piece is the critical one.
A page loads slowly and the engineering team wants to rewrite everything before anyone has profiled the actual hot path.
Someone proposes deleting the rarely used features, and nobody has checked whether admins or accessibility users depend on them.
Rank the backlog by impact times confidence divided by effort, then ask whether the bottom half could simply be cut.
Sort the crash log and support queue by frequency before triage, so the handful of bugs causing most pain surfaces first.
Segment feature usage by who rather than how many, and flag anything load-bearing for admins, oncall, or assistive technology before cutting.
